title: Rama gone, Ravana gone
hookLine: raam gaio raavan gaio: Rama went, and Ravana with his large family went too (Salok M9 50, ang 1429)

cards: Every autumn across north India, at Dussehra, crowds gather in open fields to watch giant effigies of Ravana, the ten-headed king of Lanka in the Ramayana, go up in flames. Children sit on their parents' shoulders.

Fireworks crack inside the figure. The story behind it, of Rama, the hero king, and his long war with Ravana to win back Sita, is one of the best-known stories in South Asia. Everyone in Guru Tegh Bahadur's world knew it.
So when one of his saloks opens with those two names side by side, his listeners would have sat up. What could he be saying about them?

teach.b: The fiftieth salok says raam gaio raavan gaio, jaa kau bahu parvaar. In paraphrase: Rama went, and Ravana went, who had such a large family. Says Nanak, nothing stays steady; the world is like a dream.
Parvaar is family, the whole household; Ravana, in the epic, had a vast family and kingdom.

teach.h: THE HERO AND THE PROUD ONE.
teach.b: The salok's point is very simple: the greatest hero in the story and the greatest villain both left this world. The one people worship and the one they burn. Death took both.
Here it's worth saying who believes what. For many Hindus, Rama is God come to earth, deeply loved and worshipped.

Sikh teaching speaks of God as never born and never dying, and Sikhs read this salok as being about Rama the king in the story, a man who walked the earth and left it. The salok isn't mocking anyone's faith.
It uses the most well-known names anyone knew to make the plainest point there is.
If even they went, the hero with all his virtue, the villain with all his power and his huge family, then nobody's status, goodness or strength buys a longer stay. It's not meant to make us gloomy.
It's meant to make us honest. What lasts, as these saloks keep saying, is the Name of the Lord. Even they went.

how: This salok is read near the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; Sikh teachers explain it as a reminder that even the greatest figures of the old stories departed, so no one's status lasts.

games.q: the salok sets the greatest hero and the greatest villain side by side. what does it say about them?
o: the hero lasts forever and the villain doesn't.
the villain's family kept his kingdom alive.
games.why: raam gaio raavan gaio: Rama went, Ravana went, with all his family. says Nanak, nothing stays steady; the world is like a dream.

practice: Bring to mind three people who once seemed larger than life, a well-known leader, a great artist, someone in your own family everyone looked up to, and picture each at the height of their strength.
Remember, calmly, that each has gone or will, and that your own life will pass too; then ask what you'd like to fill it with. If you pray, rest in Waheguru between breaths.
